name: Gibraltar
title: UTM Thickness Gauging in Gibraltar: Anchorage & Drydock
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Gibraltar at the anchorages and Gibdock: hull structure gauging, pre-docking surveys and checks of scrubber piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement in Gibraltar's Anchorages and Drydocks
intro: Gibraltar is where many ships pause on passage through the Strait — for bunkers, stores, crew changes, a repair period at Gibdock or a change of ownership — and as a British Overseas Territory it runs its own port and maritime administration. When a technical manager needs hull gauging in Gibraltar during that pause, we mobilise technicians from India to the Rock, work by launch or in the dock depending on where the ship lies, and hand the superintendent a readings report arranged for the class surveyor.

highlights.p: Bunkering, stores and crew-change stops at the Western and Eastern anchorages leave room for targeted gauging. We plan the spaces, permits and launch times with the agent so the team boards ready to measure.

highlights.h: Dock and anchorage in one visit
highlights.p: Gibdock and the anchorages lie close together, so one mobilisation can cover a pre-docking survey at anchor, the docking itself and a second ship waiting offshore, keeping readings consistent across phases.

Gibraltar's role as a delivery and redelivery point brings on-hire, off-hire and pre-purchase gauging. Readings are reported location by location so buyers, sellers, owners and charterers can compare them later.

port.h: Gibraltar on the Strait: bunkers, repairs and ship handovers
p: Gibraltar's port earns its living from ships that are passing rather than discharging. Its position at the eastern entrance to the Strait makes it a natural stop for vessels entering or leaving the Mediterranean, and the Gibraltar Port Authority runs a busy anchorage trade built on bunkering by barge, stores and spares delivery, crew changes and husbandry calls. Cargo handling is a small part of the picture: tankers, bulk carriers, container ships and car carriers anchor for fuel and services, then resume their voyage. Cruise ships use the cruise terminal, and the dockyard keeps a steady flow of repair work.

Two features shape inspection demand. First, Gibdock, in the former naval dockyard, gives the Rock its own drydocking and ship-repair capacity, so a ship can arrive for bunkers and stay for a docking survey without leaving the area. Second, Gibraltar is a standard delivery and redelivery point in time charters, and ships changing hands often use the anchorage for condition inspections and handover. Both bring requests for gauging — pre-docking steel estimates for Gibdock, and pre-purchase or on-hire thickness readings for buyers and charterers who want the hull condition on record at the moment responsibility changes.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with its own maritime administration and its own ship register within the Red Ensign Group, and its port and anchorages operate under Gibraltar law rather than Spain's. For a technical manager the practical points are that agents, launch services and permissions are arranged through Gibraltar's own channels, and that the drydock and the anchorages sit close together, which lets a gauging team move between a docking job and an anchorage job in the same visit. The territory is compact, the logistics are short, and the main variables are the weather in the Strait and the length of each ship's stop at anchor.

facilities.h: Gibdock, the anchorages and the berths: where Gibraltar gauging is done
p: Drydock work at Gibdock is the most complete setting for thickness gauging in Gibraltar: tanks are gas-freed and ventilated under the yard's safety system, staging or access equipment is arranged through the yard, and the bottom shell can be measured from outside once the ship is on blocks. Gibdock thickness measurement is usually split into two phases — a pre-docking or first-day survey to firm up the steel renewal list, and measurements after cleaning or blasting where the surveyor wants confirmation of what remains.

Anchorage work is done by launch, booked through the ship's agent under the Gibraltar Port Authority's rules for service craft. The Eastern Anchorage on the Mediterranean side is exposed to the Levante, and in strong easterlies launch transfers there can be suspended, so anchorage jobs carry weather float in the plan; the Western Anchorage inside the bay is more sheltered from that wind. Alongside berths are few, so most commercial ships are gauged either at anchor or in the dockyard. Gibraltar's compactness helps: a team on a docking job at Gibdock can take an anchorage job between yard shifts without a second mobilisation.
list: Gibdock drydocks — renewal and docking survey gauging, external bottom shell readings and post-blast confirmation measurements during repair periods
Western Anchorage in the Bay of Gibraltar — bunkering, stores and crew-change calls used for targeted gauging and pre-purchase sampling
Eastern Anchorage on the Mediterranean side — anchorage gauging and on-hire or off-hire condition readings, with weather float for Levante conditions
Cruise terminal berths — limited alongside work such as piping and void gauging during turnaround or repair calls
Algeciras and the Bay of Cádiz — nearby Spanish ports where the same technicians can continue if the ship's next call is across the bay or along the coast

context.h: Flag, port state and fuel rules on the Rock
p: Gibraltar's maritime affairs are handled by the Gibraltar Maritime Administration, which runs the Gibraltar Ship Registry, and by the Gibraltar Port Authority, which controls the harbour and the anchorages. Port state control and flag inspections are matters for the Gibraltar authorities rather than for Spain, and owners of Gibraltar-flagged ships deal with a register that sits alongside the UK and the other Red Ensign registers. Because Gibraltar is outside the European Union, owners whose ships trade between the Rock and EU ports should check with their compliance teams how those calls are treated for EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime.

On sulphur, Gibraltar lies within the Mediterranean SOx ECA, so the ECA limit has applied to ships here since 1 May 2025. Ships arriving from the Atlantic change over fuel or bring their scrubbers into ECA mode as they approach, and scrubber-equipped ships taking bunkers at anchor are a regular source of piping inspection work: wash-water lines, overboard discharges and the shell areas around them corrode quickly once a system has run for several years. Because Gibraltar's bunkering trade means many ships plan short stops here deliberately, it is a convenient place to slot in targeted gauging before a docking elsewhere, or to confirm a defect the crew has reported on passage.

jobs.h: What Gibraltar gauging requests usually look like
jobs.p: Work in Gibraltar falls into two groups: dockyard jobs, where gauging supports a survey and a repair specification at Gibdock, and anchorage jobs, where the ship is stopping for bunkers, a crew change or a handover. The first allows full survey scopes; the second calls for a precise list of spaces and a realistic view of what the team can cover before the ship sails. Typical requests include:
list: Pre-docking gauging of cargo hold and ballast tank structure on a bulk carrier anchored off Gibraltar, feeding the steel renewal list for its renewal survey at Gibdock.
On-hire or off-hire condition gauging at the Western Anchorage when a time charter delivers or redelivers at Gibraltar, recording deck, hatch cover and ballast tank readings for both parties.
Sale and purchase gauging on a Supramax bulk carrier lying in the anchorage during the buyer's inspection, giving the buyer hold frame, topside tank and deck readings before the sale is concluded.
Scrubber overboard and sea chest gauging on a cruise ship during a repair call at Gibdock, where readings taken from outside the hull confirm the internal measurements on the same lines.
Deck plating and hatch coaming gauging on a general cargo ship anchored for bunkers after the crew reports wastage, giving the owner readings to send to class before the voyage continues.

logistics: Technicians fly to Gibraltar International Airport via a UK connection, or to Málaga and cross the land frontier at La Línea by road. Entry rules for Gibraltar and for transit through Spain both have to be checked, and the routing chosen decides which visas the team needs, so we confirm the current requirements with the ship's agent before flights are booked. Dockyard access is arranged with Gibdock through the agent; for anchorage jobs the agent books a launch and confirms it against the ship's bunkering or service schedule. Early notice of a docking date lets the visa steps finish without squeezing the job.

faqs.q: Can gauging start at a Gibraltar anchorage and finish at Gibdock?
faqs.a: Yes, and for a ship heading into a docking survey it is often the best split. Readings in ballast tanks and accessible spaces taken at anchor before the docking give the yard and the surveyor an early steel list; the bottom shell, gas-freed cargo tanks and any areas needing post-blast confirmation are then measured in the dock. The same technicians can cover both phases, which keeps the readings consistent.

faqs.q: Is Gibraltar inside the Mediterranean ECA?
faqs.a: Yes. The western limit of the Mediterranean SOx ECA crosses the Strait near Tarifa, west of the Rock, so ships at Gibraltar's anchorages and berths have been subject to the ECA sulphur limit since 1 May 2025. For scrubber-equipped ships the system runs during the stay, and wash-water and overboard piping is worth gauging at intervals agreed with the superintendent rather than left until a leak appears.

faqs.q: Can you do on-hire or off-hire gauging when a charter delivers at Gibraltar?
faqs.a: Yes, where the ship actually stops for the handover. Condition gauging at the anchorage gives owners and charterers a shared record of hull, deck and tank thickness at the point responsibility changes. We agree the measurement locations with both sides in advance where possible, take the readings during the handover stay, and issue a report that can be attached to the on-hire or off-hire survey.

faqs.q: Do your technicians need anything special to enter Gibraltar?
faqs.a: They need the right entry documents for Gibraltar and, if they travel through Spain, a Schengen visa as well. Since our teams travel from India, we start the visa process as soon as the job is confirmed and agree a realistic boarding date with the owner and the agent. For a Gibdock docking planned weeks ahead this is straightforward; for a short-notice anchorage call it is the factor that decides whether we can attend.
